title: Short Stuff: Ellen Richards
summary: Short Stuff episode on Ellen Henrietta Swallow Richards, the American chemist who was among the first female chemists in the US and the first woman admitted to MIT's science program. The hosts frame her story within the Matilda effect, the long-standing pattern of women's scientific work being overlooked or credited to men, a term coined by historian Margaret Rossiter after abolitionist Matilda Joslyn Gage. Richards founded the field of "oekology" (ecology) in the 1870s, which MIT then told her to stop discussing, so she turned to domestic science (home economics), bringing sanitary and science-based household practices into the home. The hosts describe her advocacy for college education for women, a free chemistry lab she taught for women at MIT, and her relative obscurity today.

segments.title: Opening banter and the Matilda effect
segments.summary: The hosts introduce the episode about undersung women in science and explain the Matilda effect, the pattern of women's work being overlooked or credited to men, citing studies on journal review and abstract quality.

segments.title: Ellen Richards's education and early career
segments.summary: Richards was the first woman accepted into MIT's science program, earned a chemistry degree from Vassar in 1870 and an MIT Bachelor of Science in 1873, and began studying pollution and sanitary chemistry.

segments.title: Oekology and MIT's ban
segments.summary: Richards founded the field of oekology (ecology), studying how water, air and food affect health. MIT restricted her from discussing it for a year, and the field lasted only about five years in her work.

segments.title: Domestic science and home economics
segments.summary: Frustrated, Richards turned to domestic science, applying science-based sanitation, household organization and healthy family practices to the work women already did at home.

segments.title: Advocacy for women and legacy
segments.summary: The hosts describe Richards as a proto-feminist who advocated college education for women, ran a free chemistry lab for women at MIT, and remains largely forgotten despite her pioneering water-quality work.

segments.title: Closing and sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts praise Richards as a top-notch scientist, point listeners to a HowStuffWorks article, and invite emails.
